Application: Consumer Problem vs CE
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{APPLICATION: Consumer Problem vs CE --- same KKT recipe, different feasibility check.}}

\emph{Setup.}
\emph{(i)} \textbf{Consumer P} (one agent): $\max U(x)$ s.t.\ $p \cdot x \leq w$, $x \geq 0$.
\emph{(ii)} \textbf{CE} ($H$ agents with endowments $\omega^h$): find prices $\hat p$ and allocations $\{\hat x^h\}$ such that each agent maxes utility given $\hat p$, and markets clear.

\begin{tabular}{p{4.5cm}|p{18cm}|p{18cm}}
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Consumer Problem (1 agent)}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Competitive Equilibrium ($H$ agents)}} \\
\hline
\textbf{(1)} \emph{Write FOCs --- one per choice variable, for each agent.} \textcolor{orange}{Consumer P: $N$ FOCs total (1 agent). CE: $N \cdot H$ FOCs total ($H$ agents).} &
\textcolor{blue}{One agent, $N$ choice variables} $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{$N$ FOCs}.

$\mathcal{L} = U(x) + \lambda\bigl[w - p \cdot x\bigr]$.
\[ \boxed{\;\tfrac{\partial U(x^*)}{\partial x_i} = \lambda\, p_i \;\;\forall i = 1,\ldots,N.\;} \]
\emph{$N$ equations, each pinning down one $x_i^*$.} &
\textcolor{blue}{$H$ agents, each with $N$ choice variables} $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{$N \cdot H$ FOCs}.

Each agent $h = 1, \ldots, H$ solves \emph{their own} consumer problem with their own multiplier $\lambda^h$:
\[ \boxed{\;\tfrac{\partial U^h(x^{h*})}{\partial x_i^h} = \lambda^h\, p_i \;\;\forall i = 1, \ldots, N,\;\; \forall h = 1, \ldots, H.\;} \]
\emph{$N \cdot H$ equations: $N$ per agent, $H$ agents.}
\\
\hline
\textbf{(2)} \emph{Merge FOCs (take ratios) $\to$ optimality condition.} &
The famous optimality condition: Taking ratios of FOC$_i$ / FOC$_j$ eliminates $\lambda$:
$\underbrace{\dfrac{\partial U/\partial x_i}{\partial U/\partial x_j}}_{\substack{\text{MRS}_{i,j} = \text{internal exchange rate}\\ = -\,\text{slope indiff.\ curve}\;(\dagger,\ddagger)}} = \underbrace{\dfrac{p_i}{p_j}}_{-\,\text{slope budget}}.$

{{img:0|w=380}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{$N$-dimensional MRS.}} With $N$ goods, MRS is \emph{not} a single number --- it's a \textcolor{orange}{family of pairwise ratios}:
\[ \text{MRS}_{i,j} := \dfrac{\partial U/\partial x_i}{\partial U/\partial x_j}, \quad \text{total of } \binom{N}{2} = \tfrac{N(N-1)}{2} \text{ pairs.} \]
Optimality: \emph{every} pair satisfies $\text{MRS}_{i,j} = p_i/p_j$. Equivalently, \textcolor{orange}{all $N$ ratios $MU_i / p_i$ are equal}, with common value $\lambda$ (the multiplier).
&
Same condition for each agent. Since the RHS is \emph{common} across agents (everyone faces the same prices):
\[ \boxed{\;\text{MRS}^1 = \text{MRS}^2 = \cdots = \text{MRS}^H = \tfrac{p_i}{p_j}.\;} \]
\textcolor{orange}{MRS equalization across all agents at CE.}
You have to consider that they are takign prices as given.There is an auctioner proposing some prices, agents are giving their optimal quantities for the given prices, the prices that "work" are those for which agents maximize and markets clear. The prices are then pinned down by **market clearing** where each x is the marshallian demand of a given agent! ceteris parisbus agrgeagte scarcity of an endowmnt will bring out the relative price of that good.


Within each agent, $MU_i/p_i$ converges to $\lambda^h$ (bang-for-buck equalized across goods). \textbf{Across} agents, $\lambda^1 \neq \lambda^2$ in general --- equal $\lambda$'s is a \emph{special} case (identical utility or same final bundle ratio, e.g.\ symmetric Cobb-Douglas).

{{img:2|w=680}}
This plot is the counterpart of the FOC optimality conditions: 1) the focs are a within agent condition; and 2) it is obvious the MU cannot easily be the same across agents. 

Note how when within agent liens touch thism eans ther eis no longer and incentive to trade x for y because the dollar MB is unified!

\\
\hline
\textbf{(3)} \emph{Plug FOCs into BC $\to$ demand.} &
\]
\underline{Substitute} the FOC ratios into the BC $\Rightarrow$ each $x_i^*$ expressed in $(p, w)$ alone:
\[ \boxed{\;x_i^* = x_i^*(p, w)\;} \quad \text{(\textcolor{orange}{Marshallian demand}).} \]
\textcolor{orange}{Homogeneous of degree $0$:} $x^*(\alpha p, \alpha w) = x^*(p, w)$ for all $\alpha > 0$ --- scaling all prices and wealth leaves the budget set unchanged, so the optimum is unchanged. &
\emph{Same procedure for each agent}, but with each agent's \textcolor{blue}{own wealth} $w^h = p \cdot \omega^h$ (the value of their endowment at market prices). Result: \textcolor{orange}{individual Marshallian demands}
\[ \boxed{\;x^{h*}(p, \, p \cdot \omega^h),\;\; h = 1,\ldots,H.\;} \]
Each $x^{h*}$ inherits homogeneity of degree $0$: scaling $p$ scales $w^h$ too, so the demand is unchanged.
\\
\hline
\textbf{(4)} \emph{Feasibility check.} &
\textcolor{orange}{Embedded:} budget binds, nonneg auto from FOC. \emph{Nothing extra to check.} &
Each agent's budget is embedded. \emph{Two perspectives on aggregate feasibility} $\sum_h x_i^{h*} = \sum_h \omega_i^h$:

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{CE viewpoint (decentralized).}} Aggregate market clearing is \emph{not} a constraint in any agent's problem --- it must be \textcolor{orange}{checked separately}:
\[ \sum_h x_i^{h*}(\hat p,\, \hat p \cdot \omega^h) = \sum_h \omega_i^h \;\;\forall i. \]
These $N$ equations determine the equilibrium price vector $\hat p$.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Planner viewpoint (centralized).}} for the planner aggregate feasibility is \textcolor{orange}{embedded as a constraint from Step 1},\\
\end{tabular}

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Footnotes on MRS interpretation.}}

$(\dagger)$ \emph{Internal exchange rate.} At what rate is the consumer willing to exchange $x_2$ for $x_1$? If $\text{MRS} = 4/2 = 2$, then $MU_{x_1}$ is twice $MU_{x_2}$, so the consumer is willing to give up \textbf{2 units of $x_2$ for 1 unit of $x_1$} $=$ \textcolor{orange}{internal price ratio}.

$(\ddagger)$ \emph{Slope of indifference curve.} Along $\{U = \bar U\}$: $dU = 0 \Rightarrow MU_{x_1}\, dx_1 + MU_{x_2}\, dx_2 = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{dx_2}{dx_1} = -\dfrac{MU_{x_1}}{MU_{x_2}} = -\text{MRS}.$

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Dynamics --- trade drives convergence (concrete numerical example).}}

\emph{Setup.} Consumer has $\text{MRS}_{b,a} = 2$: internally willing to give up \textcolor{blue}{$2$ units of $A$ for $1$ unit of $B$}. Market price: \textcolor{blue}{$1$ unit of $B$ costs $2.1$ units of $A$}, i.e.\ $p_b/p_a = 2.1$.

\textbf{Step 1 (compare).} $\;\text{MRS}_{b,a} = 2 \;<\; p_b/p_a = 2.1$. Market charges \textcolor{orange}{more for $B$} than consumer values it $\Rightarrow$ $B$ is \emph{overpriced} for this consumer.

\textbf{Step 2 (trade).} Consumer \textcolor{orange}{sells $B$, buys $A$}: pay $1$ unit of $B$, receive $2.1$ units of $A$ (better than internal rate of $2$).

\textbf{Step 3 (concavity of $U$ kicks in).}
$\bullet$ Less $B$ $\;\Rightarrow\; MU_B \uparrow$ (diminishing returns; see Plot 2).
$\bullet$ More $A$ $\;\Rightarrow\; MU_A \downarrow$.
$\bullet$ Hence $\text{MRS}_{b,a} = MU_B/MU_A$ \emph{rises} toward $p_b/p_a = 2.1$.

\textbf{Step 4 (stop at tangency).} When $\text{MRS}_{b,a} = 2.1$: now to give up $1$ unit of $B$ the consumer demands $2.1$ units of $A$ in compensation --- exactly what the market pays. \emph{No further profitable trade $\Rightarrow$ optimum reached.}

nodes.title: Application: Homothetic Preferences
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{HOMOTHETIC PREFERENCES --- demand scales linearly with wealth.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Definition (primitive: scaling property of preferences).}}
Preferences are \emph{homothetic} iff for any bundles $x, y$ and any $\alpha > 0$:
\[ \boxed{\;x \sim y \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; \alpha x \sim \alpha y.\;} \]
\emph{Stated purely on the preference order $\sim$ --- the true definition.}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Characterization (corollary, functional form).}}
$U$ is homothetic iff
\[ U(x) = g\bigl(h(x)\bigr) \]
with \textcolor{blue}{$g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ strictly increasing} and \textcolor{blue}{$h: \mathbb{R}_+^N \to \mathbb{R}$ homogeneous of degree $1$}: $h(\alpha x) = \alpha\, h(x)\;\forall \alpha > 0$.

\emph{Example.} $U(x_1, x_2) = \ln x_1 + \ln x_2$: take $h(x_1, x_2) = \sqrt{x_1 x_2}$ (homogeneous degree 1) and $g(z) = 2 \ln z$. Then $g(h(x)) = 2 \ln\sqrt{x_1 x_2} = \ln(x_1 x_2) = \ln x_1 + \ln x_2 = U(x).\;✓$

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Property 1 --- MRS is constant along rays from the origin.}}

\emph{Concrete (1-good intuition).} If ``2 units of good $A$ $\sim$ 4 units of good $B$'' (exchange ratio $1{:}2$), then scaling by $\alpha = 4$: ``8 units of $A$ $\sim$ 16 units of $B$'' (still $1{:}2$). The willingness to substitute is preserved. The optimal point will have the same slope!

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Property 2 --- Indifference curves are radial scaled copies.}}

Pick a point $P = (x_1, x_2)$ on one indifference curve. Then for any $\alpha > 0$, the point $\alpha P = (\alpha x_1, \alpha x_2)$ lies on a \emph{different} indifference curve, but \emph{in the same direction} from the origin. Each indifference curve is the image of any other under a radial scaling.

{{img:0|w=720}}

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Property 3 --- Optimal consumption lies on a ray (income expansion path).}}

\emph{Claim.} If $x^*$ is optimal at prices $p$ and wealth $w$, then $\alpha x^*$ is optimal at the same prices with wealth $\alpha w$.

\emph{Proof.} Optimality: $\text{MRS}(x^*) = p_1/p_2$. By Property 1, $\text{MRS}(\alpha x^*) = \text{MRS}(x^*) = p_1/p_2$. So $\alpha x^*$ satisfies the same tangency condition. Budget: $p \cdot (\alpha x^*) = \alpha (p \cdot x^*) = \alpha w$. $\square$. The agent picks the \textcolor{orange}{same consumption ratio} (= direction in the bundle space) regardless of wealth. Wealth scales the bundle uniformly along that ray.

Corollary: $\;x_i^*(p, \alpha w) = \alpha\, x_i^*(p, w)$. Hence
\[ \boxed{\;\epsilon_{i, w} \;:=\; \dfrac{\partial \ln x_i^*}{\partial \ln w} \;=\; 1 \quad \forall i.\;} \]
\emph{Equivalently:} $x_i^*(p, w) = x_i^*(p) \cdot w$ and $v(p, w) = v(p) \cdot w$.

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why this matters: representative agent.}}
With homothetic preferences, \emph{aggregate demand depends only on total wealth, not on its distribution}:
\[ \sum_h x_i^*(p, w^h) \;=\; x_i^*(p) \cdot \sum_h w^h \;=\; x_i^*(p) \cdot W. \]
$\Rightarrow$ Replace many heterogeneous agents by a single \emph{representative agent} with total wealth $W$ --- a workhorse of macro.

\textbf{So think about the optimization:} there is a given aggregate $\omega_a/\omega_b$ ratio, and in the identical-homothetic case all agents pick the \emph{same} individual consumption ratio $x_a^h/x_b^h$ (because they share the same homothetic preferences, so ratios are wealth-independent and identical across agents). The aggregate consumption ratio --- being a sum of identical individual ratios --- equals that common individual ratio. Market clearing then forces it to equal $\omega_a/\omega_b$.

\bigskip\bigskip

nodes.title: Application: Quasilinear Preferences
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{QUASILINEAR PREFERENCES --- no wealth effect on non-numeraire goods.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Definition.}}
\[ \boxed{\;U(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N) = \alpha\, x_1 + u(x_2, \ldots, x_N), \quad \alpha > 0.\;} \]
Good 1 is the \textcolor{orange}{numeraire}: utility \emph{linear} in $x_1$, so $MU_1 = \alpha$ is \textbf{constant} (no diminishing returns). $x_1$ unrestricted in sign (``money'', will see why).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 1 --- Two structurally different FOCs.}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{FOC for $x_1$:} $\;\alpha = \lambda p_1$. \emph{Does not pin down $x_1$!}, hence $\lambda^* = \alpha/p_1$ (constant) $\Rightarrow$ marginal utility of wealth independent of $w$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{FOC for $x_i$, $i \geq 2$:} optimal quantities pinned down by prices and alfa, not depending on wealth!  $x_i^*$ for $i \geq 2$ \textcolor{orange}{independent of $w$} $\Rightarrow$ wealth elasticity $\epsilon_{i,w} = 0$ for non-numeraire goods.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 2 --- Equimarginal principle (single agent).}}

Combining the FOCs: at interior solution ( $x_1^* > 0$) note you need to check after you solev the problem that your solution is idneed interior! , every good gives the same marginal-benefit-per-dollar (``bang for buck''):
\[ \frac{MB_1}{p_1} = \frac{\alpha}{p_1} = \frac{\partial u/\partial x_i}{p_i} = \frac{MB_i}{p_i} \quad \forall i. \]
The common level is fixed by the numeraire FOC at $\alpha/p_1$. \emph{This is the floor.}

If this is an interior solution, so if $x_1 > 0$, we have that this $MB_1/p_1$ floor has been reached, and from that point on you keep buying it (or better, keep money) because the marginal utility / marginal benefit from buying a car is lower than keeping the money.

\emph{Why money absorbs extra wealth.} Buying another unit of $x_2$ pushes $MB_2/p_2$ \emph{below} $\alpha/p_1$ (concavity, $u'$ falls); keeping the dollar xas numeraire keeps $MB_1/p_1$ at the constant $\alpha/p_1$. Extra wealth flows into $x_1$ --- not because $x_1$ is intrinsically preferred, but because it's the only good whose $MB/p$ doesn't fall as you consume more.

Consequence:  $x_1^*(p, w) = w - \sum_{i\geq 2} p_i\, x_i^*(p)$, \emph{residual}: the numeraire absorbs all wealth, linear in $w$ with slope 1.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 3 --- Floor is the SAME across agents (CE with numeraire access).}}

In CE, every agent with $x_1^h > 0$ has $\lambda^h = \alpha^h/p_1$. With identical preferences (same $\alpha$), the floor is identical:
\[ \boxed{\;\frac{MB_i^h}{p_i} = \frac{\alpha}{p_1} \quad \forall h,\, \forall i.\;} \]
Bang-for-buck unified across goods \emph{and} across agents, that is, they all have the same MRS. 

\textbf{Critical implication.} Same $MB/p$ across agents does \textbf{not} mean same $x_1$ (numeraire); it means same $x_2$ (non-numeraire, since $\partial u/\partial x_2 = \alpha p_2$ pins a common $x_2^*$ when preferences are identical). All wealth differences go into $x_1$. 


Interior $\Rightarrow$ $x_2^*$ independent of endowment $\Rightarrow$ same $x_2^*$ for all individuals $\Rightarrow$ Marshallian doesn't depend on wealth, personal demand is unchaned in endowments $\Rightarrow$ prices s.t. dpend on a marshallian indepenent of welath, so are indpeendent of endowment distribution, the idea is that no change in eprsonal demand is generatign no change in aggregate demand hence no change in prices. 

{{img:1|w=1100}}





\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 4 --- Geometric reading.}}
Indifference curves are \textcolor{orange}{horizontal translates} of one another (shifted along the $x_1$ axis). MRS depends \emph{only} on $(x_2, \ldots, x_N)$:
\[ \text{MRS}_{i,1} = \dfrac{\partial u/\partial x_i}{\alpha} \quad\text{(no $x_1$ in it).} \]

{{img:0|w=720}}


\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Worked example: same problem, two endowment configurations.}}

\emph{Setup.} $U^h(x_1, x_2) = \alpha\, x_1 + \ln(x_2)$ with $\alpha = 1$, $p_1 = 1$ (numeraire). Two configurations:

nodes.title: CE equilibrium visualized
nodes.content:
\textbf{Correct.} Aggregate $\omega_a/\omega_b$ does NOT enter Marshallian demand as a function. It enters CE only through the \textbf{market-clearing equation}, which is what pins down prices. After prices are solved, plugging them back into Marshallian demand gives the actual quantities.

{{img:0|w=1100}}

\textbf{Key element (central red rectangle):} the equation $\sum_h x_a^h(p, w^h) = \omega_a$ is where the model's \emph{two threads} meet: Marshallian demand $x_a^h(p, w^h)$ on the LHS (coming in from the right, function of prices), and aggregate $\omega_a$ on the RHS (coming in from the left, primitive). Solving the equation pins $\hat p$. \emph{Only then} can we plug $\hat p$ back into Marshallian demand to get numerical $x^{h*}$.

Note how the given p gives you a specific demand point.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{IDENTICAL vs HETEROGENEOUS homothetic --- two layers of the ``homothetic result''.}}

\emph{Two distinct properties involved:}
\textbf{(i)} \textcolor{blue}{Individual homotheticity:} for each agent, $x_a^h/x_b^h$ depends only on prices, not on $w^h$. \emph{Per-agent.}
\textbf{(ii)} \textcolor{blue}{Same $r^*(p)$ across agents:} all agents share the same demand-ratio function. \emph{Population-level.}

The famous ``aggregate pins prices'' and ``individual ratio $=$ aggregate ratio'' results require \textbf{both}. Drop (ii) but keep (i) and the aggregate-level results break; the individual-level properties survive.

\emph{Common setup:} $\omega^1 = (5, 1),\, \omega^2 = (1, 4),\, \omega = (6, 5)$.

\begin{tabular}{p{4cm}|p{10cm}|p{10cm}}
 & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Col 2: IDENTICAL homothetic}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Col 3: HETEROGENEOUS homothetic}} \\
\textit{Preferences} & both $U^h = x_a^{0.4} x_b^{0.6}$ & $U^1 = x_a^{0.2} x_b^{0.8}$, $\;U^2 = x_a^{0.8} x_b^{0.2}$ \\
\textit{Each agent homothetic?} & \textcolor{green}{✓} & \textcolor{green}{✓} \\
\textit{Same $r^*(p)$ across agents?} & \textcolor{green}{✓} & \textcolor{red}{✗} \\
\hline
\textbf{(1) Agent $h$'s problem.}
$\max U^h$ s.t.\ $p_a x_a + p_b x_b = w^h$, where $w^h = p_a \omega_a^h + p_b \omega_b^h$. &
\emph{Identical Marshallian structure in both columns;} &
\emph{the difference is only in $U^h$ (see row above).} \\
\hline
\textbf{(2) FOCs} (one per good) &
$0.4\, x_a^{-0.6} x_b^{0.6} = \lambda^h p_a$
$0.6\, x_a^{0.4} x_b^{-0.4} = \lambda^h p_b$
\emph{(same form for both agents)} &
Agent 1 ($\alpha = 0.2$): $0.2 \,x_a^{-0.8} x_b^{0.8} = \lambda^1 p_a$, $\,0.8\, x_a^{0.2} x_b^{-0.2} = \lambda^1 p_b$.
Agent 2 ($\alpha = 0.8$): $0.8\, x_a^{-0.2} x_b^{0.2} = \lambda^2 p_a$, $\,0.2\, x_a^{0.8} x_b^{-0.8} = \lambda^2 p_b$. \\
\hline
\textbf{(3) Ratio of FOCs} (kill $\lambda^h$) $\to$ $r^*(p)$ &
$\dfrac{x_a^h}{x_b^h} = \dfrac{0.4}{0.6}\,\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} = \dfrac{2}{3}\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} \equiv r^*(p).$
\textcolor{orange}{Same function for both agents.} &
Agent 1: $\dfrac{x_a^1}{x_b^1} = \dfrac{0.2}{0.8}\,\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} = \dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} \equiv r_1^*(p).$
Agent 2: $\dfrac{x_a^2}{x_b^2} = \dfrac{0.8}{0.2}\,\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} = 4\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} \equiv r_2^*(p).$
\textcolor{red}{Different functions: $r_1^* \neq r_2^*$.} \\
\hline
\textbf{(4) FOC ratio $+$ budget} $\to$ \emph{Marshallian demand}.
Take budget $p_a x_a^h + p_b x_b^h = w^h$ (with $w^h = p_a \omega_a^h + p_b \omega_b^h$ known), and plug in $p_b/p_a$ from the FOC ratio (Step 3) to eliminate one variable. &
$r^*(p) = \tfrac{2}{3}\tfrac{p_b}{p_a}$.
$p_a r^* + p_b = \tfrac{2}{3} p_b + p_b = \tfrac{5}{3} p_b.$
$x_b^h \cdot \tfrac{5}{3} p_b = w^h \;\Rightarrow\; x_b^h = \tfrac{3}{5}\dfrac{w^h}{p_b} = \dfrac{0.6\, w^h}{p_b}.$
$x_a^h = r^*(p)\, x_b^h = \tfrac{2}{3}\tfrac{p_b}{p_a} \cdot \tfrac{3}{5}\tfrac{w^h}{p_b} = \dfrac{0.4\, w^h}{p_a}.$
\textcolor{orange}{Same coefficient $0.4$ on $w^h$ for both agents.} &
\emph{Agent 1} ($r_1^* = \tfrac{1}{4}\tfrac{p_b}{p_a}$): $p_a r_1^* + p_b = \tfrac{1}{4} p_b + p_b = \tfrac{5}{4} p_b.$
$x_b^1 = \tfrac{4}{5}\dfrac{w^1}{p_b} = \dfrac{0.8\, w^1}{p_b}.\;\;x_a^1 = r_1^* x_b^1 = \dfrac{0.2\, w^1}{p_a}.$
\emph{Agent 2} ($r_2^* = 4\tfrac{p_b}{p_a}$): $p_a r_2^* + p_b = 4 p_b + p_b = 5 p_b.$
$x_b^2 = \tfrac{1}{5}\dfrac{w^2}{p_b} = \dfrac{0.2\, w^2}{p_b}.\;\;x_a^2 = r_2^* x_b^2 = \dfrac{0.8\, w^2}{p_a}.$
\textcolor{red}{Different coefficients on $w^h$ across agents.} \\
\hline
\textbf{(5) Market clearing for $A$} \emph{(the pivot step)} &
$\sum_h x_a^h = \dfrac{0.4 (w^1 + w^2)}{p_a} = \omega_a$
$\Rightarrow 0.4\,(p_a \omega_a + p_b \omega_b) = p_a \omega_a$
$\Rightarrow 0.4(6 p_a + 5 p_b) = 6 p_a$
$\Rightarrow 2 p_b = 3.6 p_a.$
\textcolor{orange}{Truly depends on aggregate $\omega$!} &
$\sum_h x_a^h = \dfrac{0.2\, w^1 + 0.8\, w^2}{p_a} = \omega_a$
$\Rightarrow 0.2(5 p_a + p_b) + 0.8(p_a + 4 p_b) = 6 p_a$
$\Rightarrow 1.8 p_a + 3.4 p_b = 6 p_a$
$\Rightarrow 3.4 p_b = 4.2 p_a.$
\textcolor{red}{Individual $\omega^h$ enter \emph{separately}.} \\
\hline
\textbf{(6) Equilibrium prices} &
$\hat p_b/\hat p_a = 3.6/2 = 1.8.$
\emph{Normalize:} $\hat p_a = 1$, $\hat p_b = 1.8.$ &
$\hat p_b/\hat p_a = 4.2/3.4 \approx 1.235.$
\emph{Normalize:} $\hat p_a = 1$, $\hat p_b \approx 1.235.$ \\
\hline
\textbf{(7) Wealths at CE} &
$w^1 = 5 + 1.8 = 6.8$, $w^2 = 1 + 7.2 = 8.2$. &
$w^1 = 5 + 1.235 = 6.235$, $w^2 = 1 + 4.94 = 5.94$. \\
\hline
\textbf{(8) Individual demands and ratios} &
$x^1 = (0.4 \cdot 6.8,\, 0.6 \cdot 6.8 / 1.8) = (2.72,\, 2.267)$.
$x^2 = (3.28,\, 2.733)$.
\emph{Ratios:} $2.72/2.267 = 1.2$;\; $3.28/2.733 = 1.2$.
\textcolor{orange}{Both $= \omega_a/\omega_b = 1.2$.} &
$x^1 \approx (0.2 \cdot 6.235,\; 0.8 \cdot 6.235 / 1.235) \approx (1.247,\, 4.039)$.
$x^2 \approx (4.752,\, 0.962)$.
\emph{Ratios:} $1.247/4.039 \approx 0.31$;\; $4.752/0.962 \approx 4.94$.
\textcolor{red}{Wildly different; neither $= 1.2$.} \\
\hline
\textbf{(*) Swap test} \;($\omega^1 \leftrightarrow \omega^2$, same aggregate) &
Identical agents $\Rightarrow$ swapping is a relabel: clearing equation \emph{unchanged}.
$\hat p_b/\hat p_a = 1.8$ (\textcolor{green}{unchanged}).
\textcolor{orange}{Distribution irrelevant.} &
After swap: $0.2(p_a + 4 p_b) + 0.8(5 p_a + p_b) = 6 p_a \Rightarrow 4.2 p_a + 1.6 p_b = 6 p_a \Rightarrow \hat p_b/\hat p_a = 1.125$.
\textcolor{red}{Prices change from $1.235$ to $1.125$.}
Distribution \textcolor{red}{matters}. \\
\end{tabular}

\bigskip

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{In the specific context of this question: why is the aggregate endowment ratio equal to the optimal individual consumption ratio?}}

\emph{The point:} agents are identical and homothetic, so each one wants a fixed consumption ratio $x_a^h/x_b^h$ (wealth-independent, and the \emph{same} across agents). The only feasible value of that common ratio --- i.e., the only one for which prices exist that clear the market --- is the one matching the aggregate endowment ratio $\omega_a/\omega_b$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Proof.}}

\emph{Step 1 --- personal Marshallian consumption ratio} (from Step 3 of the table):
\[ \dfrac{x_a^*}{x_b^*} \;=\; \dfrac{2}{3}\,\dfrac{p_b}{p_a}. \]
\textcolor{orange}{Note: independent of wealth} --- this is the homothetic property.

\emph{Step 2 --- market clearing for $A$ pins prices:}
\[ \sum_h x_a^h \;=\; \dfrac{0.4\,(w^1 + w^2)}{p_a} \;=\; \omega_a, \]
with $w^1 + w^2 = p_a \omega_a + p_b \omega_b$. Substituting:
\[ 0.4\,(p_a \omega_a + p_b \omega_b) \;=\; p_a \omega_a \;\Longrightarrow\; 0.4\, p_b \omega_b \;=\; 0.6\, p_a \omega_a \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\;\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} \;=\; \dfrac{3}{2}\,\dfrac{\omega_a}{\omega_b}.\;} \]

\emph{Step 3 --- plug equilibrium prices back into the Marshallian ratio:}
\[ \dfrac{x_a^*}{x_b^*} \;=\; \dfrac{2}{3}\,\dfrac{p_b}{p_a} \;=\; \dfrac{2}{3} \cdot \dfrac{3}{2}\,\dfrac{\omega_a}{\omega_b} \;=\; \boxed{\;\dfrac{\omega_a}{\omega_b}.\;} \quad\square \]

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Read.}} The Marshallian ratio is a function of prices alone (Step 1). Market clearing then forces prices to satisfy a specific relation with $\omega_a/\omega_b$ (Step 2), and that relation is exactly the inverse of the Marshallian coefficient $2/3$. The two effects cancel, leaving $x_a^*/x_b^* = \omega_a/\omega_b$. The cancellation is not a coincidence --- it is what \emph{forces} the common individual ratio to coincide with the aggregate one whenever (i) and (ii) both hold.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Same CE template, completely instantiated --- every equation and number from the comparison table is visible.}}

\emph{Common setup:} $\omega^1 = (5, 1),\, \omega^2 = (1, 4),\, \omega = (6, 5)$. Each box shows its symbolic label (green) and its concrete content (blue). \textbf{Crucially:} the Marshallian-demand box shows only the \emph{functional form} in terms of $p$ --- no numerical $x^*$ values appear there, since those require knowing equilibrium $\hat p$ (which is what the central red rectangle solves).

\textbf{Reading the schema.} Steps (1)-(2)-(3)-(4) flow from the right side (primitives $\to$ FOC/BC $\to$ Marshallian demand). Step (5)-(6) is the central red rectangle: market clearing solves for $\hat p$. Below the central rectangle the chain continues: (7) wealths at CE $\to$ (8) numerical demands and ratios $\to$ ($*$) swap test.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Case 2: identical homothetic}} --- $U^h = x_a^{0.4} x_b^{0.6}$ for both. Result: $\hat p_b/\hat p_a = 1.8$, both individual ratios collapse to $1.2 = \omega_a/\omega_b$. Swap test: prices unchanged (distribution irrelevant). $\checkmark$

{{img:0|w=1200}}


Note how prices reflect scarcity! $\frac{\omega_a}{\omega_b} = \frac{P_b}{P_a} * \frac{2}{3}$
\bigskip

Crucial: note how the marshallian depend on $\frac{P_b}{P_a}$ in both a direct and indirect way: 1) direct effect is the income effect and the subsitutio effect, 2) indirect effect is the weallth effect 3) interestingly there is no effect of Pa on Xb: they exacly cancel out, this is a specific of Cobb douglas only. The primitive boxes (endowments, preferences) feed BC and FOC, which feed the Marshallian box, which feeds the central market-clearing rectangle. The only thing that changes is the content of $U^h$ --- and that propagates downstream into different FOCs, different Marshallian formulas (Step 3 ratios $r^*$ collapse vs.\ diverge), different central clearing equations (aggregate-only vs.\ individual-$\omega^h$-dependent), different equilibrium prices, different wealths, and (the punchline) wildly different individual demand ratios in the output box.

nodes.title: Representative Agent Assumption
Application: Real Endowments --- the Endowment Slutsky Equation
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{REAL ENDOWMENTS --- when wealth itself depends on prices.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setup: nominal vs.\ real wealth.}}

\emph{Usual textbook problem (nominal wealth).} The consumer is given $(p, w)$ \emph{exogenously}. Wealth $w$ is just a number, unrelated to prices. The Marshallian demand $x_i^*(p, w)$ is a function of these two independent arguments.

\emph{Real-endowment problem (this snippet).} The consumer owns physical quantities --- the \emph{real endowment vector} $\omega = (\omega_1, \ldots, \omega_N)$ --- and faces market prices $p$. Their wealth is then \emph{endogenously determined} by the value of what they own:
\[ \boxed{\;w(p) \;=\; p \cdot \omega \;=\; \sum_j p_j\, \omega_j.\;} \]
The relevant demand is now the \emph{endowment-economy demand}: substitute the wealth identity into the Marshallian formula,
\[ \hat x_i^*(p, \omega) \;:=\; x_i^*\bigl(p,\; p \cdot \omega\bigr). \]
This is the demand of an agent who owns $\omega$ and trades in markets at prices $p$ --- the natural object for a CE.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 1 --- The chain rule: two channels for a price change.}}

When $p_j$ rises, the consumer feels it \emph{twice}: directly through the demand formula at fixed wealth, and indirectly through the value of their endowment. By the chain rule:
\[ \boxed{\;\dfrac{\partial \hat x_i^*(p, \omega)}{\partial p_j} \;=\; \underbrace{\dfrac{\partial x_i^*(p, w)}{\partial p_j}\bigg|_{w\text{ fixed}}}_{\text{Marshallian price effect}} \;+\; \underbrace{\dfrac{\partial x_i^*(p, w)}{\partial w} \cdot \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial p_j}}_{\text{endowment-wealth effect}}.\;} \]
And since $w = p \cdot \omega$, $\partial w/\partial p_j = \omega_j$. So:
\[ \dfrac{\partial \hat x_i^*}{\partial p_j} \;=\; \dfrac{\partial x_i^*}{\partial p_j}\bigg|_{w} \;+\; \omega_j \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_i^*}{\partial w}. \]
The agent gets ``richer'' when the price of a good they own rises --- by exactly $\omega_j$ extra dollars per unit of $p_j$ change.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 2 --- The first term IS the standard Slutsky decomposition.}}

\emph{Yes:} the first term $\partial x_i^*/\partial p_j$ at fixed $w$ is exactly the \textbf{Marshallian (uncompensated) price effect}, which by the classical Slutsky equation splits into a substitution effect and a (Marshallian) income effect:
\[ \boxed{\;\dfrac{\partial x_i^*(p, w)}{\partial p_j}\bigg|_{w} \;=\; \underbrace{\dfrac{\partial x_i^h(p, \bar U)}{\partial p_j}}_{\text{substitution } S_{ij}} \;-\; \underbrace{x_j^*(p, w) \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_i^*}{\partial w}}_{\text{Marshallian income effect}}.\;} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Intuition.}}

You were at equilibium, here you had $Mb_a / p_a = Mb_b / p_b $

Two things happen \emph{simultaneously}:

- (A) Now $Mb_a / p_a < Mb_b / p_b$, you sell apples and you buy bread until again  $Mb_a / p_a = Mb_b / p_b $.  \textbf{substitution effect}. In the budget $x_a^h + \underbrace{p_b/p_a}_{\text{here}} x_b^h = w^h/p_a$  you see the relative prices changing (budget rotates), hence this affect the optimum marshallilan quantities. Note that with just a change of slope you stay on the SAME INDIFFERENCE CURVE. Indeed, there is no loss, prices are different, and you fix your internal exchange rate to the external one, as for you the budget line is steeper andyouw ant to sell x and buy y now. 

- (B) But also $x_a^h +p_b/p_a x_b^h =  \underbrace{w^h/p_a}_{\text{here}}$ the overall budget line shifts in, with the same money of before you can afford less bundles than before \textbf{income effect}. This alfo affects the optimum marshallian quantities. 

- But you observe a mix of the two. How to disentangle the two: Imagine I hand you \emph{just enough extra w} (note the amount of compensation dpeends on how much you cared for Apples and how much the price increases, if you really cared and do not think bread is a subsitte and the price increase in apples is high, we will need to give you a lot of moeny ) so you could still reach your original Indifference curve. There I neutralzied B  and i can just observe A. Then If estiamte the sub effectm I can just remove the subsidy and observe just the effect of the downward shift in the budget.

nodes.title: Indirect utility + roy identity
Application: Labor Supply Elasticities (General, Frisch, Applied)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{LABOR SUPPLY ELASTICITIES --- general, Frisch, applied:}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setup.}}
\[ \max_{c, h} \;U(c) - v(h) \quad\text{s.t.}\quad c = w h + I, \;\; c, h > 0. \]
$U$ concave in $c$, $v$ convex in $h$. Lagrangian (multiplier $\lambda$ on the budget):
\[ \mathcal{L} = U(c) - v(h) - \lambda\,(c - w h - I). \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Question.}} How does the optimal hours $h^*$ respond to a wage change?
\[ \boxed{\;\epsilon_{h, w} \;:=\; \dfrac{\partial h^*}{\partial w} \cdot \dfrac{w}{h^*}.\;} \]



\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Reminder: every FOC step starts by setting the relevant partial of $\mathcal{L}$ to $0$.}}

\textbf{Notation:} the multiplier $\lambda^*$ depends on the \emph{exogenous} parameters of the Lagrangian $(w, I)$ --- never on the endogenous choice variables $c, h$ (they get absorbed into $c^*(w, I), h^*(w, I)$ after solving).

\begin{tabular}{p{7cm}|p{13cm}|p{10cm}|p{10cm}}
\textbf{Step} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{GENERAL}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{FRISCH ($\bar\lambda$ fixed)}} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{APPLIED}  $v(h) = h^{1+1/\epsilon}/(1+1/\epsilon)$, $U(c) = c$} \\
\hline
\textbf{(1) Retrieve $h^*$} from FOC w.r.t.\ $h$. &
\textbf{FOC$_h$:} $-v'(h^*) + \lambda^*(w, I)\, w = 0$
$\Rightarrow v'(h^*(w, I)) = w \lambda^*(w, I)$

A wage change has two channels:

$\bullet$ \textcolor{blue}{Direct ($+\Delta w$):} higher wage $\to$ more work.
$\bullet$ \textcolor{blue}{Indirect / income ($-\Delta w$):} $\lambda^* \downarrow$ (richer $\to$ less marginal value of $c$) $\to$ work less. &
\textbf{FOC$_h$:} $-v'(h^*) + \bar\lambda\, w = 0$
$\Rightarrow v'(h^*) = w \bar\lambda$

\emph{(no income effect: $\bar\lambda$ fixed by assumption $\Rightarrow$ only the direct channel survives)} &
\textbf{FOC$_h$:} $-h^{*\,1/\epsilon} + \bar\lambda\, w = 0$
$\Rightarrow h^*(w, \lambda) = (w \lambda)^{\epsilon}$ \\
\hline
\textbf{(2) Find $\lambda^*$} from FOC w.r.t.\ $c$. &
\textbf{FOC$_c$:} $U'(c^*) - \lambda^* = 0$
$\Rightarrow \lambda^*(w, I) = U'(c^*(w, I))$
\emph{(depends on $w, I$ through $c^*$)} &
\emph{No need;} $\bar\lambda$ fixed by assumption. &
\textbf{FOC$_c$:} $1 - \lambda^* = 0$
\emph{(since $U(c) = c \Rightarrow U'(c) = 1$)}
$\Rightarrow \lambda^* = \bar\lambda = 1$ \\
\hline
\textbf{(3) Compute $\partial h^*/\partial w$.} Differentiate FOC$_h$ (and FOC$_c$, FOC$_{BC}$ where needed) w.r.t.\ $w$. &
From FOC$_h$ (product rule): $v''(h^*)\, \dfrac{\partial h^*}{\partial w} = \lambda^*(w, I) + w\, \boxed{\dfrac{\partial \lambda^*}{\partial w}}$

\emph{Need} $\boxed{\partial \lambda^*/\partial w}$. From FOC$_c$ (chain rule): $\boxed{\dfrac{\partial \lambda^*}{\partial w}} = U''(c^*)\, \boxed{\dfrac{\partial c^*}{\partial w}}$

\emph{Need} $\boxed{\partial c^*/\partial w}$. From FOC$_{BC}$ (product rule): $\boxed{\dfrac{\partial c^*}{\partial w}} = h^* + w\, \dfrac{\partial h^*}{\partial w}$
 &
From FOC$_h$ (with $\partial \bar\lambda/\partial w = 0$):
$v''(h^*)\, \dfrac{\partial h^*}{\partial w} = \bar\lambda$ &
Direct from $h^*(w, \bar\lambda) = (w\bar\lambda)^{\epsilon}$:
$\dfrac{\partial h^*}{\partial w} = \epsilon\, \bar\lambda^{\epsilon}\, w^{\epsilon - 1}$ \\
\hline
\textbf{(4) Convert to elasticity:} multiply by $w/h^*$. &
Substitute (FOC$_c$, FOC$_{BC}$) into the differentiated FOC$_h$ and solve:
$\boxed{\;\epsilon_{h, w} = -\dfrac{U'(c^*) + h^* w\, U''(c^*)}{w^2 U''(c^*) - v''(h^*)} \cdot \dfrac{w}{h^*}\;}$ &
$\epsilon^{F}_{h, w} = \dfrac{\underbrace{\bar\lambda\, w}_{v'(h^*)}}{v''(h^*)\, h^*}$
 &
$\epsilon^{*}_{h, w} = \epsilon\, \bar\lambda^{\epsilon} w^{\epsilon - 1} \cdot \dfrac{w}{(w \bar\lambda)^{\epsilon}}$
$\Rightarrow \boxed{\;\epsilon^{*}_{h, w} = \epsilon\;}$ \\
\end{tabular}

nodes.title: Planner's Problem (linear SWF) — characterization of PO
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{PLANNER'S PROBLEM --- characterize PO via a linear social welfare function.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Linear social welfare function.}} For $\lambda \in (0, 1)$:
\[ \boxed{\;[\mathrm{A}]:\quad \max_{(x^1, x^2) \in \mathcal{F}} \;\;\lambda\, U^1(x^1) + (1-\lambda)\, U^2(x^2).\;} \]
$\lambda$ encodes the planner's preference weight on agent 1 vs.\ agent 2.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Solving $[\mathrm{A}]$.}} Pick $\lambda$, write Lagrangian with feasibility constraints, FOCs (\emph{set partial derivatives to $0$}), solve. The output is a single utility pair --- a UPF point. Sweeping $\lambda \in (0, 1)$ traces out the UPF.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Theorems linking $[\mathrm{A}]$ and PO.}}

\textbf{(i) Sufficient.} If $(\bar x^1, \bar x^2)$ solves $[\mathrm{A}]$ for some $\lambda \in (0, 1)$ (interior; otherwise the planner only weights one guy), then $\bar x$ is PO.

\textbf{(ii) Necessary (under concavity).} If $\bar x$ is PO \emph{and} each $U^i$ is concave and increasing, then $\exists \lambda \in (0, 1)$ s.t.\ $\bar x$ solves $[\mathrm{A}]$.

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Note on (ii).}} Concavity is crucial to retrieve \emph{all} PO points via $\lambda$. Without concavity, some PO points (sitting on non-convex parts of the UPF) cannot be retrieved by any $\lambda$ --- the planner's tangent isowelfare line skips over kinks/holes. See \emph{CE failures} for the non-convexity issue.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Cross-references.}} Built on \emph{PO} and \emph{UPS/UPF}. The planner's prices are the tangent slope $-\lambda/(1-\lambda)$, which connects to \emph{Second Welfare Theorem}.

nodes.title: Contract Curve — PS restricted to endowment-improving
Competitive Equilibrium — definition + solve process
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{COMPETITIVE EQUILIBRIUM (CE) --- prices and allocation where markets clear and consumers optimize.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Definition.}} A pair $(\hat p, \hat x)$ with $\hat p \in \mathbb{R}^N_+$ and $\hat x = (\hat x^1, \ldots, \hat x^I)$ such that:

\textbf{1) Consumer optimization:} for every agent $i$,
\[ \boxed{\;\hat x^i \;\in\; \arg\max_{x^i \geq 0} U^i(x^i) \;\;\text{s.t.}\;\; \hat p \cdot x^i \leq \hat p \cdot \omega^i.\;} \]

\textbf{2) Market clearing:} for every good $n$,
\[ \boxed{\;\sum_{i=1}^I \hat x_n^i \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^I \omega_n^i \;=\; \omega_n.\;} \]

Under strictly increasing preferences, the budget constraint binds with equality.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Solve process (smooth interior case).}}
\textbf{1)} Write each agent's optimization problem.
\textbf{2)} Take FOCs and \emph{set them to $0$}: MRS$^i = \hat p_a / \hat p_b$ for each $i$.
\textbf{3)} Solve for individual demand $x^i(p)$ from FOCs $+$ budget.
\textbf{4)} Impose market clearing for one good (Walras' Law gives the other automatically) and solve for $\hat p$.
\textbf{5)} Plug $\hat p$ back into individual demands to get $\hat x$.

{{img:0|w=900}}

\emph{Reading the Edgeworth picture.} Endowment $\omega = (8, 2)$ for agent 1, $(2, 6)$ for agent 2. Budget line through $\omega$ with slope $-\hat p_a/\hat p_b$. The CE allocation is the unique point where \emph{both} agents' ICs are tangent to the budget line (MRS$^1$ = MRS$^2$ = $\hat p_a/\hat p_b$) --- hence on the contract curve.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Conditions for existence.}}
$\bullet$ \textcolor{blue}{Continuity} of preferences.
$\bullet$ \textcolor{blue}{Strict monotonicity} (consumers want more).
$\bullet$ \textcolor{blue}{Strict convexity} (consumers prefer averages, concave $U^i$).
Under these, a CE exists. Failures arise when these break --- see \emph{CE failures}.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Cross-references.}} \emph{First Welfare Theorem} (every CE is PO). \emph{Second Welfare Theorem} (any PO supported as CE with transfers). \emph{CE failures} (when CE doesn't exist). \emph{Application: Homothetic / Quasilinear / Cobb-Douglas Preferences} (worked CE examples).

nodes.title: First Welfare Theorem (FWT) — CE → PO
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FIRST WELFARE THEOREM --- every CE is Pareto Optimal.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Statement.}} If $(\hat p, \hat x)$ is a Competitive Equilibrium \emph{and} each $U^i$ is strictly increasing in every good, then $\hat x$ is Pareto Optimal.

\[ \boxed{\;\text{CE} \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \text{PO}\quad \text{(under strict monotonicity)}.\;} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Proof sketch.}}
\textbf{(i)} Suppose for contradiction $\hat x$ is not PO. Then $\exists y \in \mathcal{F}$ with $U^i(y^i) \geq U^i(\hat x^i)$ $\forall i$ and strict for some $j$.
\textbf{(ii)} Strict monotonicity $+$ consumer optimization at prices $\hat p$:
$\bullet$ For agent $j$ (strictly better off): $\hat p \cdot y^j > \hat p \cdot \hat x^j$ (otherwise $y^j$ would have been chosen).
$\bullet$ For other agents: $\hat p \cdot y^i \geq \hat p \cdot \hat x^i$.
\textbf{(iii)} Sum: $\hat p \cdot \sum_i y^i \;>\; \hat p \cdot \sum_i \hat x^i$. By feasibility of $y$ and market clearing: $\sum_i y^i = \omega = \sum_i \hat x^i$. Contradiction $\Rightarrow$ $\hat x$ is PO. $\quad\square$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Key takeaway.}} CE allocations are always on the \emph{Pareto Set} (and in fact on the \emph{Contract Curve}, since they're individually rational by construction). The market efficiently rules out wasteful allocations \emph{without a planner}.

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{What FWT does NOT say.}}
$\bullet$ CE allocations need not be \emph{fair}. The endowment distribution determines who gets what at the CE.
$\bullet$ CE allocations are PO \emph{only if} CE exists. See \emph{CE failures} for when it doesn't.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Cross-references.}} \emph{CE definition}, \emph{Pareto Optimum}, \emph{Contract Curve}. The converse (PO $\Rightarrow$ CE) requires more --- see \emph{Second Welfare Theorem}.

nodes.title: Second Welfare Theorem (SWT) — PO → CE with transfers
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SECOND WELFARE THEOREM --- any PO can be supported as a CE with lump-sum transfers.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Statement.}} Under \emph{convexity of preferences} (concave $U^i$), \emph{strict monotonicity}, and continuity: \emph{any} Pareto-optimal allocation $\bar x$ can be supported as a CE relative to some prices $\hat p \in \mathbb{R}^N_+$ \emph{after} lump-sum transfers $T = (T^1, \ldots, T^I)$ with $\sum_i T^i = 0$.

\[ \boxed{\;\text{Any PO} \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \text{CE} \;\;\text{with transfers (under convexity)}.\;} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Proof sketch.}}
\textbf{(i)} Take any PO $\bar x$ with utilities $\bar u^i = U^i(\bar x^i)$.
\textbf{(ii)} \emph{Separating hyperplane theorem.} Define the upper-contour sets $V^i = \{x^i : U^i(x^i) \geq \bar u^i\}$. Under convexity, $\sum_i V^i$ is convex. Since $\bar x$ is PO and feasibility is binding, the aggregate endowment $\omega$ lies on the boundary of $\sum_i V^i$. $\Rightarrow$ $\exists$ a hyperplane (with normal vector $\hat p$) supporting $\sum_i V^i$ at $\omega$.
\textbf{(iii)} These supporting prices $\hat p$ are the CE prices: at $\hat p$, every $\bar x^i$ is utility-maximizing in agent $i$'s budget set.
\textbf{(iv)} Choose transfers $T^i = \hat p \cdot (\bar x^i - \omega^i)$ to make $\bar x^i$ affordable for agent $i$ at prices $\hat p$. $\sum_i T^i = 0$ by feasibility. $\;\square$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Reading the picture (Edgeworth box).}} At any PO interior point, the two agents' ICs are tangent. The \emph{slope of the common tangent} = $-\hat p_a / \hat p_b$ = supporting prices. Transfers shift the budget line so it passes through the desired PO bundle instead of through the original endowment.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why this matters.}}
$\bullet$ \textcolor{orange}{Equity-efficiency separation.} The planner can pick the most equitable PO and \emph{implement it via the price mechanism} just by redistributing endowments. Market efficiency and distributional choice are separable.
$\bullet$ \textcolor{orange}{Decentralization.} A planner doesn't need to choose individual allocations --- they just set transfers and let markets clear.

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Caveat.}} Without convexity (concave preferences), the separating hyperplane argument fails. Some PO points lie on non-convex parts of the UPF and cannot be supported by any prices. See \emph{CE failures}.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Cross-references.}} \emph{CE definition}, \emph{Pareto Optimum}, \emph{Contract Curve}, \emph{Planner's Problem} (the prices are the planner's tangent isowelfare slope), \emph{First Welfare Theorem} (the converse direction).

nodes.title: CE failures — when no equilibrium exists
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{CE FAILURES --- three classic ways CE may fail to exist.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Big picture.}} PO \emph{always} exists under continuity. CE may fail. But if CE exists, it is always PO (by FWT). The three classic failures break one of the existence conditions: monotonicity, convexity, satiation/boundedness.

{{img:0|w=1100}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Failure 1 --- Non-convex preferences (concave ICs).}}
With non-convex upper-contour sets, the demand correspondence is \emph{discontinuous}: tiny price changes cause big jumps in demand. Aggregate excess demand $z(p)$ has jumps, so $z(p) = 0$ may have no solution.

\emph{Geometric intuition.} The upper-contour set is non-convex $\Rightarrow$ no separating hyperplane $\Rightarrow$ no price vector supports a given PO. SWT also fails here.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Failure 2 --- Non-monotonic preferences.}}
If one agent doesn't value one of the goods (flat IC over that dimension), they don't want to trade for it. Markets cannot clear because there's no positive price at which the indifferent agent supplies/demands the good.

\emph{Example.} Agent 1 has standard preferences over both goods. Agent 2 is indifferent to good $b$ (only cares about $a$). Endowment at a boundary where agent 2 owns $b$. Agent 2 has no reason to trade $b$ for anything. Agent 1 cannot find prices that let them buy $b$ without making agent 2 strictly worse off.

\emph{Geometric:} flat ICs $\Rightarrow$ MRS is $0$ or $\infty$ $\Rightarrow$ no smooth tangency $\Rightarrow$ no interior CE.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Failure 3 --- Boundary / non-satiation.}}
If, at $p_n = 0$, demand for good $n$ is unbounded (e.g.\ lexicographic preferences, Inada-style with no finite max), markets cannot clear at $p_n = 0$. And at $p_n > 0$ some other failure occurs (e.g.\ corner endowments).

\emph{Concrete sketch.} Suppose agent 1 has $\omega^1 = (0, 1)$, agent 2 has $\omega^2 = (1, 0)$, with preferences that produce infinite demand at $p_n = 0$:
$\bullet$ If $p_n = 0$ for some $n$: infinite demand from someone $\to$ market doesn't clear.
$\bullet$ If $p_a > 0, p_b > 0$: at the unique candidate budget, one agent (call them agent 2) is not at their global optimum --- they'd prefer to stay at the endowment $A$. So the candidate $(\hat p, \hat x)$ isn't actually a CE.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Important takeaway.}} Even when CE fails, \emph{PO still exists}. The Pareto Set is well-defined under continuity alone. The failure of CE is about the \emph{price mechanism} not being able to support the Pareto-optimal outcomes --- not about efficiency being undefined.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Cross-references.}} \emph{CE definition} (existence conditions). \emph{Pareto Optimum} (always exists). \emph{Second Welfare Theorem} (also fails when convexity breaks).

nodes.title: Exchange Economy — setting and feasibility
Pareto Optimum --- PS and UPF (dual views)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{PARETO OPTIMUM --- UPF and PS, the two coordinate views.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(1) UPF --- where it lives.}}
$\mathrm{UPF} \subset \mathcal{U}$, where
\[ \mathcal{U} \;=\; \bigl\{(u^1, u^2) \;:\; \exists\, x \in \mathcal{F},\; U^i(x^i) \geq u^i \;\forall i\bigr\} \]
is the set of \emph{utility profiles dominated by some feasible allocation}.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(2) UPF --- definition (no domination).}}
$(\bar u^1, \bar u^2) \in \mathcal{U}$ is on the UPF iff
\[ \boxed{\;\nexists\, (\tilde u^1, \tilde u^2) \in \mathcal{U} : \tilde u^i \geq \bar u^i \;\forall i,\; > \text{some } j.\;} \]
set of utiliteis that are undominated

{{img:0|w=580}}

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{(4) PS --- definition (no domination).}}
$\bar x \in \mathcal{F}$ is Pareto Optimal iff
\[ \boxed{\;\nexists\, y \in \mathcal{F} : U^i(y^i) \geq U^i(\bar x^i) \;\forall i,\; > \text{some } j.\;} \]
and $\mathrm{PS} = \{x \in \mathcal{F} : x \text{ is PO}\}$. Basically is an allocaiton taht cannot e dominated.

\textcolor{orange}{\emph{The allocation-space picture (Edgeworth box) lives in its own snippet --- ``PS in the Edgeworth box''.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(5) Finding PS $\equiv$ finding UPF.}}
The two problems are equivalent via the utility map: every $x^* \in \mathrm{PS}$ pushes forward to a UPF point, and every UPF point is the image of some $x^* \in \mathrm{PS}$. Formally:
\[ \boxed{\;\mathrm{PS} \;\subset\; \mathcal{F} \;\;\xrightarrow{\;(U^1,\, U^2)\;}\;\; \mathrm{UPF} \;\subset\; \mathcal{U}.\;} \]

\textcolor{orange}{\emph{Comment: the UPF is the set of all PO allocations viewed in utility coordinates instead of allocation coordinates.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(6) Two characterizations of \textbf{PS}.}}

\emph{Why planner}: both characterizations are written from the viewpoint of a benevolent social planner who picks an allocation $x \in \mathcal{F}$ to maximize a welfare objective. The planner will hence choose to stay on the PS / UPF.

\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{(6a) Linear scalarization --- weighted SWF.}}
\[ \boxed{\;[\mathrm{A}]:\;\; x^*(\lambda) \;=\; \arg\max_{x \in \mathcal{F}}\; \lambda\, U^1(x^1) + (1-\lambda)\, U^2(x^2),\qquad \lambda \in (0, 1).\;} \]
So imagine you have this whole points in teh blue space, and you want to find the points on the frontier. The object above is a straight line ()

Planner uses a linear SWF $W = \lambda U^1 + (1-\lambda)U^2$, weighting agent $i$ by $\lambda$ vs.\ $1-\lambda$. Once you rearrange you get $-\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda} u^1 + \underbrace{\frac{w}{1 - \lambda}}_{K},$ so $\lambda$ tilts the planner's preferences: $\lambda \to 1$ favors agent 1, $\lambda \to 0$ favors agent 2.

{{img:0|w=580}}

\textbf{Solve (one-line Lagrangian).} Just follow KKT procedure to solve the problem! 

\textbf{Proof that $x^*(\lambda) \in \mathrm{PS}$ (concise).} Suppose $y \in \mathcal{F}$ Pareto-dominates $x^*$: $U^i(y^i) \geq U^i(x^{*i})\;\forall i$ with strict somewhere. Contraddiction! $\blacksquare$

\textcolor{orange}{\textbf{Note.} This proves \emph{every solution of $[\mathrm{A}]$ is in PS}. The converse --- sweeping $\lambda \in (0,1)$ retrieves \emph{all} of PS / UPF --- is a \emph{further step} requiring concave $U^i$ (so $\mathcal{U}$ is convex and every UPF point has a supporting hyperplane).}

\textbf{From PS to UPF.} Once $x^*(\lambda)$ is in hand, the corresponding UPF point is $\bigl(U^1(x^{1*}),\, U^2(x^{2*})\bigr)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{darkgreen}{(6b) Constrained max --- UPF as an explicit function.}}
\[ \boxed{\;[\mathrm{B}]:\;\; P(\bar u^1) \;=\; \max_{x \in \mathcal{F}}\; U^2(x^2) \quad\text{s.t.}\quad U^1(x^1) \geq \bar u^1.\;} \]
Planner fixes agent 1 at floor $\bar u^1$ and maximizes agent 2. Sweep $\bar u^1$ across $[u^1_{\min}, u^1_{\max}]$ to trace the UPF as an explicit decreasing function $P(\cdot)$.

\textbf{Solve (one-line Lagrangian).} $\mathcal{L} = U^2(x^2) + \mu\bigl(U^1(x^1) - \bar u^1\bigr) - \sum_n \nu_n\bigl(\sum_i x_n^i - \omega_n\bigr)$. FOCs give again $\mathrm{MRS}^1 = \mathrm{MRS}^2$. The shadow price $\mu = -P'(\bar u^1)$ is the slope of UPF at $\bar u^1$, and $\mu = \lambda/(1-\lambda)$ links the two characterizations.

\textbf{Proof (concise).} If $y \in \mathcal{F}$ Pareto-dominates $x^*$, then $U^1(y^1) \geq U^1(x^{*1}) \geq \bar u^1$ (so $y$ is feasible for $[\mathrm{B}]$) and $U^2(y^2) > U^2(x^{*2})$, contradicting optimality of $x^*$. $\blacksquare$

\textbf{From PS to UPF.} $(\bar u^1, P(\bar u^1)) \in \mathrm{UPF}$.

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Example --- one-good economy.}} $N = 1$ good, endowment $\omega$, $U^i$ strictly increasing.
\[ P(\bar u^1) \;=\; \max_{x^1, x^2 \geq 0}\; U^2(x^2) \;\text{ s.t. }\; U^1(x^1) \geq \bar u^1,\; x^1 + x^2 = \omega. \]
Strict monotonicity $\Rightarrow$ the utility constraint binds: $x^1 = (U^1)^{-1}(\bar u^1)$, then $x^2 = \omega - x^1$, so
\[ \boxed{\;P(\bar u^1) \;=\; U^2\bigl(\omega - (U^1)^{-1}(\bar u^1)\bigr).\;} \]
\emph{Reading:} the one-good UPF is a strictly decreasing curve parametrized by how the planner splits $\omega$ between agents. PS in allocation space is the segment $\{(x^1, \omega - x^1) : x^1 \in [0, \omega]\}$ --- every split is efficient.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(7) Existence and convexity.}}
$\bullet$ \emph{Existence}: $\mathrm{PS} \neq \emptyset$ (hence $\mathrm{UPF} \neq \emptyset$) under \textcolor{orange}{continuity of utilities alone} --- no monotonicity, convexity, or differentiability needed.
$\bullet$ \emph{Convexity}: concave $U^i$ $\Rightarrow$ $\mathcal{U}$ convex $\Rightarrow$ every UPF point has a supporting hyperplane $\Rightarrow$ the iff in (6a) holds and SWT goes through.
$\bullet$ \emph{Fairness}: PS says nothing about distribution (giving all $\omega$ to one agent is a PO). PS depends only on preferences, not on $\omega$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(8) Four facts to remember.}}
\textbf{1)} \textbf{Same set, two views.} PS and UPF are the same object in $(x_1, x_2)$ vs.\ $(u^1, u^2)$ coordinates; the utility map shuttles between them.
\textbf{2)} \textbf{Isowelfare slope} $-\lambda/(1-\lambda)$: the planner's tangent slope on UPF equals the supporting price ratio at the corresponding PS bundle.
\textbf{3)} \textbf{FOC at smooth interior PO:} $\mathrm{MRS}^1 = \mathrm{MRS}^2$ --- the same condition emerges from both characterizations.
\textbf{4)} \textbf{Existence is cheap.} Continuity alone $\Rightarrow$ PS and UPF exist; convexity gives retrieval and SWT.

\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Cross-references.}}
$\bullet$ \emph{PS in the Edgeworth box} --- allocation-space picture; each PO point sits on the UPF.
$\bullet$ \emph{Exchange Economy} --- foundation, defines $\mathcal{F}$.
$\bullet$ \emph{Planner's Problem} --- theorems linking $[\mathrm{A}]$ to PO.
$\bullet$ \emph{Contract Curve} --- subset of PS individually rational w.r.t.\ $\omega$.
$\bullet$ \emph{FWT} (CE $\Rightarrow$ PO) and \emph{SWT} (PO $\Rightarrow$ CE with transfers, uses the supporting price slope).
